encounters.cc: presents to the emergency department with rapidly worsening skin pain and widespread areas of peeling over the past 2 days

lines: She presents to the emergency department with rapidly worsening skin pain and widespread areas of peeling over the past 2 days

The patient is a 44-year-old female with a history of glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism diagnosed in April 2020 and morbid obesity evaluated in January 2020 who presents to the emergency department with rapidly worsening skin pain and widespread areas of peeling over the past 2 days.
She reports that she initially developed a low-grade fever and sore throat approximately one week ago and was prescribed an oral medication at an urgent care clinic.
Three days after starting the medication, she developed a diffuse, erythematous rash across her trunk and face that progressed to involve her upper extremities.
Over the last 24 hours, she has had increasing pain in her mouth, eyes, and genital area, with difficulty eating, photophobia, and burning on urination.
She also reports malaise, chills, and generalized body aches.
She denies recent travel, new foods, or known environmental exposures.
Her past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension and seasonal allergic rhinitis.
Medications include hydrochlorothiazide and a recently prescribed antibiotic.
- Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) 10 cm H2O nightly
Sulfonamide antibiotics (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) - Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis, Pollen (seasonal)
- Familial hyperaldosteronism type I (autosomal dominant) in father and paternal grandmother
- Premature coronary artery disease (father, myocardial infarction at age 48)
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Administrative assistant.
On examination, her temperature is 38.9°C (102.0°F), blood pressure is 102/66 mm Hg, pulse is 112/min, and respirations are 20/min.
Her face appears erythematous and swollen, with crusting at the lips and multiple erosions inside the oral mucosa.
There is bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge.
Her chest and back reveal coalescing erythematous macules with flaccid bullae and areas of skin sloughing on gentle pressure.
Similar findings are noted on the arms and upper thighs.
The genital mucosa appears erythematous and denuded in some areas.
Laboratory studies reveal mild leukopenia and elevated transaminases.
Blood cultures and viral PCR panels are pending.
A chest radiograph shows no pulmonary infiltrates.

encounters.cc: 6-month history of progressive blurring of vision, particularly when reading or using a computer, and difficulty seeing in dim light

lines: 6-month history of progressive blurring of vision, particularly when reading or using a computer, and difficulty seeing in dim light
The patient is a 45-year-old female with glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism and history of toxic epidermal necrolysis who presents with progressive visual symptoms.
Over six months, she has noted progressive blurring, particularly when reading or using a computer, with difficulty in dim light.
She also reports noticing a dark spot in the center of her vision that seems to move as she looks around.
Her past medical history includes hypertension, which has been poorly controlled, and hyperlipidemia.
- Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) 10 cm H2O nightly
Sulfonamide antibiotics (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) - Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis, Pollen (seasonal)
- Familial hyperaldosteronism type I (autosomal dominant) in father and paternal grandmother
- Premature coronary artery disease (father, myocardial infarction at age 48)
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Administrative assistant.
On physical examination, her visual acuity is 20/40 in both eyes, and there is no afferent pupillary defect.
She sees wavy lines on an Amsler grid test.
Fundoscopic examination reveals exudates and microaneurysms in the macula, with hard drusen and a subretinal hemorrhage.
Fluorescein angiography shows patchy areas of hypofluorescence.

She denies any changes in bowel habits or urine color.
Her past medical history is significant for hyperlipidemia and obesity.

lines: She comes to the emergency department with 2 days of worsening abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting

She reports mild subjective fevers and chills but no changes in bowel habits.
She has no history of recent travel, alcohol abuse, or liver disease.

She has had three prior pregnancies without complications.
